newsitem.title: UK: LME copper dips, but spreads still full of steam.
newsitem.headline: LME copper dips, but spreads still full of steam.

text.p: An impasse between longs and squeezed shorts kept nearby LME copper dates stubbornly firm on Thursday afternoon as three months prices dipped, traders said.
The premium of cash over three months finished the day at $198/$203 per tonne, up from $160/$170 on Wednesday and barely off its peak of $210 during the morning session.
"There are still a lot of shorts out there," one trader said.
The ability of the spreads to stay resilient while the three month market eased from highs indicated that the shorts are merely rolling over positions, he added.
Three months prices found difficulty near $2,400, hitting a peak in the morning just $1 below the psychological mark.
Prices dipped in the afternoon as buying dried up but then steadied and ended the afternoon kerb virtually unchanged at $2,368, up $1.
The churning market should continue for a few weeks as the squeezed dates come to maturity, traders said.
Trading is expected to be volatile on Monday as the first tight date at the end of April is traded, they added.
Players were still wary of selling or going short against a background of supply problems.

Some workers were still on strike at Chile's huge Escondida mine and management have given final wage offers to employees at Cominco's Quebrada Blanca mine, also in Chile, and at Phelps Dodge's Chino mine in the U.S.
A Kennecott smelter is down for maintenance work for six weeks and output in Zambia has fallen.
Analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis said there is a potential for lost output of up to 40,000 to 50,000 tonnes.
Other markets lost some steam after following copper higher and overextending themselves.
Aluminium looked a bit tired after failing to maintain a foothold above $1,600 even after its substantial stock declines recently, including 3,250 tonnes on Thursday.
Prices touched $1,615, but the 30-day moving average just below there provided stiff resistance and prices edged back to close the day at $1,594, a $7.50 loss.
Nickel hit $7,550 but came back with copper and the others to end the kerb down $25 at $7,450.
The market needs to close above $7,520 to break out of its current range, analysts said.
Zinc, which along with nickel is seen as fundamentally stronger than some of the others, hit $1,288 before the afternoon blues hit the complex. Last kerb business was down $12 at $1,271.
Lead held to a tight $5 range, finishing off $3 at $636 while tin took a $90 dive to close at $5,720, below its 10-day moving average.
Alloy was last indicated at $1,485/88 versus $1,490/94.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
